These changes may be attenuated or delayed by hormones from endog-

DISORDERS OF DEVELOPMENT
Milk Line Remnants
Supernumerary nipples or breasts result from the persistence of epider-
mal thickenings along the milk line, which extends from the axilla to the
perineum. Breast disorders only very rarely arise in these heterotopic
foci, which most commonly come to attention due to painful swelling
prior to menstruation.
Accessory Axillary Breast Tissue
In some females the normal ductal system extends into the subcutaneous
tissue of the chest wall or the axillary fossa (the axillary tail of Spence).
Because this tissue may not be removed by prophylactic mastectomies,
such procedures markedly reduce, but do not eliminate, the risk of breast
cancer.
Congenital Nipple Inversion
The failure of the nipple to evert during development is common and
may be unilateral. Congenitally inverted nipples are usually of little
significance since they correct spontaneously during pregnancy or may
sometimes be everted by simple traction. Acquired nipple retraction is
CHAPTER 23  The Breast 945
of more concern since it may indicate the presence of an invasive cancer
or an inflammatory nipple disease.
CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS OF BREAST DISEASE
The  most  common  breast  signs  and  symptoms  reported  by
females are “lumpiness,” pain, palpable mass, nipple discharge,
and inflammatory changes (Fig. 23.2A). Symptoms are usually not
severe enough to require treatment and the primary reason for in-
vestigating their cause is to evaluate the possibility of malignancy.
Greater than 90% of symptomatic breast lesions are benign. Of fe-
males with cancer, about 45% have symptomatic disease, while the
remainder  come  to  attention  through  mammographic  screening
(Fig. 23.2B). The principal mammographic signs of breast carcinoma
are densities and calcifications. Among the most common or signifi-
cant signs and symptoms that bring breast lesions to clinical atten-
tion are:
•  Lumpiness, or diffuse nodularity of the breast, is usually a manifes-
tation of normal glandular tissue or fibrocystic changes. When
pronounced, imaging studies may be needed to exclude the pres-
ence of a discrete mass.
•  Pain (mastalgia or mastodynia) is a common symptom that may be
cyclic with menses or noncyclic. Diffuse cyclic pain may be due to
premenstrual edema. Noncyclic pain is usually localized to one area
of the breast and may be caused by a ruptured cyst, physical injury,
or  infection,  but  often  no  specific  lesion  is  identified.
Although most painful masses are benign, in about 5% of cases
the underlying cause is breast cancer.
•  Palpable masses may arise from proliferations of stromal cells or
epithelial cells and are generally detected when 2 to 3 cm in size.
Most (,95%) are benign; these tend to be discrete masses that are
round or oval, rubbery, and mobile. The most common benign
masses are fibroadenomas and cysts. In contrast, because malignant
tumors invade across tissue planes they tend to be irregular, hard
(scirrhous), and nonmobile. The likelihood that a mass is malig-
nant increases with age, rising from 10% for females under age 40
to 60% for females over age 50. Approximately 50% of carcinomas
occur in the upper outer quadrant, 10% in each of the remaining
quadrants, and about 20% in the central or subareolar region. Al-
though about one-third of cancers are first detected as a palpable
mass, screening by palpation has little effect on breast cancer mor-
tality, as most cancers with the capacity to metastasize do so before
they reach a palpable size.
•  Nipple discharge may be normal when small in quantity and bilat-
eral. Milky discharge (galactorrhea) is associated with elevated pro-
lactin levels (e.g., due to pituitary adenoma), hypothyroidism, and
endocrine anovulatory syndromes, and may also occur in patients
taking oral contraceptives, tricyclic antidepressants, methyldopa, or
phenothiazines. Repeated nipple stimulation may also induce lacta-
tion. Galactorrhea is not a feature of malignancy. Bloody or serous
discharges are most commonly due to large duct papillomas and
cysts. During pregnancy, rapid growth and remodeling of the breast
may produce a bloody discharge. Nipple discharge in older females
that is spontaneous, unilateral, and bloody is likely to  be due to
malignancy Discharge associated with malignancy is most com-
monly due to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and increases in
prevalence with age; it is caused by an underlying carcinoma in 7%
of females under age 60 years and in 30% of females 60 years of age
or older.
•  Inflammation causes erythema and edema involving all or part of a
breast. This is most often caused by infections, which only occur
with any frequency during lactation and breastfeeding.

946 CHAPTER 23 The Breast
Fig. 23.2 Symptoms of breast disease and presentations of breast cancer. (A) Common breast-related symptoms that bring patients to clinical attention include “lumpiness,” pain, palpable mass, nipple discharge, and
inflammation. Although these symptoms often cause concern, they are associated with cancer in less than
10% of affected females. (B) Presentations of breast cancer. Of females with cancer, about 65% come to
attention through mammographic screening, while the remainder have symptomatic disease.
The combination of careful clinical assessment, imaging, and biopsy
(core biopsy and/or fine needle aspiration cytology) identifies greater
than 99.5% of breast malignancies in patients with symptomatic breast
disease.
INFLAMMATORY DISORDERS
Inflammatory diseases of the breast are rare (accounting for less than 1%
of breast symptoms) and are caused by infections, autoimmune disease,
or foreign body–type reactions to extravasated keratin or secretions. Inflammatory breast cancer mimics inflammation clinically and should
always be considered in a female with an erythematous swollen breast.
Acute Mastitis
Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the first month of
breastfeeding (lactational mastitis) and is caused by a local infection
when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the
nipples. From this portal of entry, Staphylococcus aureus or less commonly streptococci invade the breast tissue. The breast is erythematous
and painful, and fever is often present. At the outset only one duct
system or sector of the breast is involved. If not treated, the infection
may spread to the entire breast. Staphylococcal infection often leads to
single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.
Most cases of lactational mastitis are effectively treated with appropriate antibiotics and continued expression of milk from the breast.
Only rarely is surgical drainage required.
Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts
Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts is known by a variety of names,
including recurrent subareolar abscess, periductal mastitis, and Zuska
disease. Females (and sometimes males) present with a painful erythematous subareolar mass that mimics a bacterial abscess. In recurrent cases, a
fistula tract often develops under the smooth muscle of the nipple and
opens onto the skin at the edge of the areola. In many affected females the
nipple inverts due to traction produced by inflammation and scarring.
More than 90% of afflicted individuals are smokers. It has been suggested
that a relative deficiency of vitamin A associated with toxic substances in
tobacco smoke alters the differentiation of the ductal epithelium.
MORPHOLOGY
The key feature is keratinizing squamous metaplasia, which extends into
the nipple duct well past the usual point of transition from squamous to glandular epithelium (Fig. 23.3). Keratin shed from these cells is trapped and plugs
affected ducts, causing ductal dilation and eventual rupture. An intense
chronic granulomatous inflammatory response develops once keratin spills into
the surrounding periductal tissue. With recurrences, secondary anaerobic
bacterial infections may supervene and cause acute inflammation.
Simple incision drains the abscess cavity, but the offending keratinizing epithelium remains and recurrences are common. In most cases,
en bloc surgical removal of the involved duct and contiguous fistula
tract is curative. If secondary bacterial infection is present, antibiotics
also have a therapeutic role.

toms that bring patients to clinical attention include “lumpiness,” pain, palpable mass, nipple discharge, and
inflammation. Although these symptoms often cause concern, they are associated with cancer in less than

attention through mammographic screening, while the remainder have symptomatic disease.
The combination of careful clinical assessment, imaging, and biopsy
(core biopsy and/or fine needle aspiration cytology) identifies greater
than 99.5% of breast malignancies in patients with symptomatic breast
disease.
INFLAMMATORY DISORDERS
Inflammatory diseases of the breast are rare (accounting for less than 1%
of breast symptoms) and are caused by infections, autoimmune disease,
or foreign body–type reactions to extravasated keratin or secretions. In-
flammatory breast cancer mimics inflammation clinically and should
always be considered in a female with an erythematous swollen breast.
Acute Mastitis
Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the first month of
breastfeeding (lactational mastitis) and is caused by a local infection
when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the
nipples. From this portal of entry, Staphylococcus aureus or less com-
monly streptococci invade the breast tissue. The breast is erythematous
and painful, and fever is often present. At the outset only one duct
system or sector of the breast is involved. If not treated, the infection
may spread to the entire breast. Staphylococcal infection often leads to
single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading in-
fection in the form of cellulitis.
Most cases of lactational mastitis are effectively treated with appro-
priate antibiotics and continued expression of milk from the breast.
Only rarely is surgical drainage required.
Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts
Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts is known by a variety of names,
including recurrent subareolar abscess, periductal mastitis, and Zuska
disease. Females (and sometimes males) present with a painful erythema-
tous subareolar mass that mimics a bacterial abscess. In recurrent cases, a
fistula tract often develops under the smooth muscle of the nipple and
opens onto the skin at the edge of the areola. In many affected females the
nipple inverts due to traction produced by inflammation and scarring.
More than 90% of afflicted individuals are smokers. It has been suggested
that a relative deficiency of vitamin A associated with toxic substances in
tobacco smoke alters the differentiation of the ductal epithelium.
MORPHOLOGY
The key feature is keratinizing squamous metaplasia, which extends into
the nipple duct well past the usual point of transition from squamous to glan-
dular epithelium (Fig. 23.3). Keratin shed from these cells is trapped and plugs
affected ducts, causing ductal dilation and eventual rupture. An intense
chronic granulomatous inflammatory response develops once keratin spills into
the surrounding periductal tissue. With recurrences, secondary anaerobic
bacterial infections may supervene and cause acute inflammation.
Simple incision drains the abscess cavity, but the offending keratin-
izing epithelium remains and recurrences are common. In most cases,
en bloc surgical removal of the involved duct and contiguous fistula
tract is curative. If secondary bacterial infection is present, antibiotics
also have a therapeutic role.

Duct Ectasia
Duct ectasia presents as a palpable periareolar mass that is often associ-
ated with thick, white nipple secretions and occasionally with skin retrac-
tion. Pain and erythema are uncommon. This disorder tends to occur in
the fifth or sixth decade of life in multiparous females. Unlike squamous
metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not associated with cigarette smoking.
MORPHOLOGY
Ectatic dilated ducts are filled with inspissated secretions and numerous lipid-
laden  macrophages.  Duct  rupture  stimulates  a  periductal  and  interstitial
chronic inflammatory reaction consisting of lymphocytes, macrophages, and
variable numbers of plasma cells (Fig. 23.4). Granulomas may form around
cholesterol deposits and secretions. Subsequent fibrosis produces an irregular
mass with skin and nipple retraction. The principal significance of duct ectasia
is that it may be difficult to distinguish on clinical and radiologic grounds from
invasive carcinoma.
Fat Necrosis
The presentations of fat necrosis may closely mimic cancer. It may
come to attention as a painless palpable mass, skin thickening or re-
traction, or mammographic densities or calcifications. About half of
affected females have a history of breast trauma or surgery.
MORPHOLOGY
Acute lesions may be hemorrhagic and contain central areas of liquefactive fat
necrosis with neutrophils and macrophages. Over subsequent days, proliferat-
ing fibroblasts and chronic inflammatory cells surround the injured area; giant
cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin then appear, and eventually the lesion is
replaced by scar tissue or is encircled and walled off by fibrous tissue. Ill-defined,
firm, gray-white nodules containing small chalky-white foci are seen grossly.
Lymphocytic Mastopathy (Sclerosing Lymphocytic
Lobulitis)
This condition presents with single or multiple hard palpable masses or
mammographic densities. The masses are associated with areas of
densely collagenized stroma, a feature that may make it difficult to
obtain lesional tissue by needle biopsy. Within the stroma are atrophic
ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes surrounded by

ectatic duct filled with inspissated debris. The fibrotic response can pro-
duce a firm irregular mass that mimics invasive carcinoma on palpation
or mammogram.

and is hypothesized to have an autoimmune basis. Its only clinical
significance is that it must be distinguished from breast cancer.
Granulomatous Mastitis
Granulomatous inflammation of the breast may be a manifestation of
systemic granulomatous diseases (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangi-
itis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) or infectious disorders localized to the
breast. Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that
occurs only in parous females. The granulomas are closely associated
with lobules and may contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils.
A similar histologic pattern is seen in cystic neutrophilic granulomatous
mastitis, which is often caused by lipophilic Corynebacteria. These his-
tologic patterns may be manifestations of the same disease. Treatment
includes antibiotics and sometimes steroids. Localized infections by
mycobacteria or fungi are rare and are most common in immunocom-
promised patients or adjacent to foreign objects such as breast prosthe-
ses or nipple piercings.

antibiotics, steroids, or surgery.

matory disorder should always be considered.
•  Majority of cases of periductal mastitis are associated with smoking, which
is thought to damage the ducts.

paragraphs: Duct Ectasia

Duct ectasia presents as a palpable periareolar mass that is often associated with thick, white nipple secretions and occasionally with skin retraction. Pain and erythema are uncommon. This disorder tends to occur in
the fifth or sixth decade of life in multiparous females. Unlike squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not associated with cigarette smoking.
MORPHOLOGY

Ectatic dilated ducts are filled with inspissated secretions and numerous lipid-laden macrophages. Duct rupture stimulates a periductal and interstitial chronic inflammatory reaction consisting of lymphocytes, macrophages, and variable numbers of plasma cells (Fig. 23.4). Granulomas may form around cholesterol deposits and secretions. Subsequent fibrosis produces an irregular mass with skin and nipple retraction. The principal significance of duct ectasia is that it may be difficult to distinguish on clinical and radiologic grounds from invasive carcinoma.
Fat Necrosis

The presentations of fat necrosis may closely mimic cancer. It may come to attention as a painless palpable mass, skin thickening or retraction, or mammographic densities or calcifications. About half of affected females have a history of breast trauma or surgery.
MORPHOLOGY

Acute lesions may be hemorrhagic and contain central areas of liquefactive fat necrosis with neutrophils and macrophages. Over subsequent days, proliferating fibroblasts and chronic inflammatory cells surround the injured area; giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin then appear, and eventually the lesion is replaced by scar tissue or is encircled and walled off by fibrous tissue. Ill-defined, firm, gray-white nodules containing small chalky-white foci are seen grossly.
Lymphocytic Mastopathy (Sclerosing Lymphocytic
Lobulitis)

This condition presents with single or multiple hard palpable masses or mammographic densities. The masses are associated with areas of densely collagenized stroma, a feature that may make it difficult to obtain lesional tissue by needle biopsy. Within the stroma are atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes surrounded by

Fig. 23.4 Duct ectasia. Chronic inflammation and fibrosis surround an ectatic duct filled with inspissated debris. The fibrotic response can produce a firm irregular mass that mimics invasive carcinoma on palpation or mammogram.

a lymphocytic infiltrate. This condition is most common in females with type 1 diabetes (diabetic mastopathy) or Hashimoto thyroiditis and is hypothesized to have an autoimmune basis. Its only clinical significance is that it must be distinguished from breast cancer.
Granulomatous Mastitis

Granulomatous inflammation of the breast may be a manifestation of systemic granulomatous diseases (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) or infectious disorders localized to the breast. Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that occurs only in parous females. The granulomas are closely associated with lobules and may contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils.

A similar histologic pattern is seen in cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, which is often caused by lipophilic Corynebacteria. These histologic patterns may be manifestations of the same disease. Treatment includes antibiotics and sometimes steroids. Localized infections by mycobacteria or fungi are rare and are most common in immunocompromised patients or adjacent to foreign objects such as breast prostheses or nipple piercings.
KEY CONCEPTS
Inflammatory Disorders
• Inflammatory diseases of the breast are rare outside of the lactational period.
• The specific cause must be determined, as appropriate treatment may be antibiotics, steroids, or surgery.
• The possibility of inflammatory carcinoma mimicking a nonneoplastic inflammatory disorder should always be considered.
• Majority of cases of periductal mastitis are associated with smoking, which is thought to damage the ducts.
• Granulomatous lobular mastitis is often idiopathic.

Another “nonproliferative” morphological alteration is lactational
adenoma, which presents as a palpable mass in pregnant or lactating
females  and  regresses  after  cessation  of  breastfeeding.  Lactational
adenomas consist of normal-appearing breast tissue with lactational
changes  and  may  be  an  exaggerated  local  response  to  gestational
hormones rather than true neoplasms.
Proliferative Breast Disease Without Atypia
Lesions characterized by proliferation of epithelial cells, without
atypia, are associated with a small increase in the risk of subsequent
carcinoma in both breasts. They are commonly detected as mammo-
graphic densities, calcifications, or incidental findings in biopsies per-
formed for other reasons. These lesions are considered predictors of risk
rather than direct precursors of carcinoma.
MORPHOLOGY
Several morphologically distinct patterns of proliferative breast disease without
atypia are recognized:
•  Usual ductal hyperplasia. Compared to normal terminal duct lobular
units (Fig. 23.6A and C), there is an increased number of both luminal and
myoepithelial cells filling and distending ducts and lobules (Fig. 23.6B and
D). Irregular lumens can often be seen at the periphery of the cellular
masses. Usual ductal hyperplasia is typically an incidental finding.
•  Sclerosing adenosis. This is a glandular proliferation characterized by an
increased number of acini that are compressed and distorted by stromal
fibrosis. On occasion, stromal fibrosis completely compresses the lumens to
create the appearance of solid cords or double strands of cells lying within
dense stroma, a pattern that superficially resembles invasive carcinoma
(Fig. 23.7). Sclerosing adenosis may come to attention as a palpable mass,
a radiologic density, or calcifications.
•  Radial scar (radial sclerosing lesion). This small stellate lesion closely
mimics invasive carcinoma mammographically, grossly, and histologically
(Fig. 23.8). The term radial scar is a misnomer as it is not associated with
prior trauma or surgery. These lesions have a central nidus of entrapped
glands in a hyalinized elastotic stroma surrounded by long radiating projec-
tions of glandular elements that may have components of sclerosing adeno-
sis, cysts, papilloma, and usual ductal hyperplasia. Complex sclerosing
lesion is defined as a radial scar larger than 1 cm in size.
•  Papilloma. Papillomas grow within a dilated duct and are composed of
multiple branching fibrovascular cores (Fig. 23.9). Usual ductal hyperplasia
and apocrine metaplasia are frequently present within the lesion. Large duct
papillomas occur centrally in the lactiferous sinuses of the nipple and are
usually solitary. Small duct papillomas are commonly multiple and located
within the peripheral ductal system. More than 80% of large duct papillomas
produce nipple discharge, which may be bloody due to torsion of the stalk,
leading to infarction. Serous discharge results from intermittent blockage and
release of normal breast secretions or irritation of the duct by the papilloma.
Most small duct papillomas are clinically occult but they may come to atten-
tion as small palpable masses or mammographic densities or calcifications.
Gynecomastia
Gynecomastia (enlargement of the male breast) is the only benign lesion
seen with any frequency in the male breast. It presents as a button-like
subareolar enlargement and may be unilateral or bilateral. Microscopi-
cally, there is an increase in dense collagenous connective tissue associ-
ated with epithelial hyperplasia of the duct lining (Fig. 23.10). Lobule
formation is almost never observed.
Gynecomastia  occurs  due  to  an  imbalance  between  estrogens,
which stimulate breast tissue, and androgens, which counteract these
effects. It may appear during puberty, in the very aged, or at any time
during adult life when there is cause for hyperestrinism. The most
important of these is cirrhosis of the liver, the organ responsible for
metabolizing estrogen. In older males, gynecomastia may stem from a
relative increase in estrogens as testicular androgen production falls.
Drugs such as alcohol, marijuana, heroin, antiretroviral therapy, and
anabolic steroids have been associated with gynecomastia. Rarely, gy-
necomastia occurs as part of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY karyo-
type) or in association with functioning testicular neoplasms, such as
Leydig cell or Sertoli cell tumors.
Proliferative Breast Disease With Atypia (Atypical
Hyperplasia) and Precursor Lesions
Breast cancer precursor lesions are noninvasive neoplastic epithelial
proliferations with the biologic potential to progress to malignancy.

aRelative risk is the likelihood of developing invasive carcinoma compared
to females without any risk factors. Absolute lifetime risk is the percentage
of females expected to develop invasive carcinoma in the absence of an
intervention.
KEY CONCEPTS
Benign Epithelial Proliferations and Precursor Lesions
• Benign epithelial proliferations and precursor lesions usually do not cause symptoms but are frequently detected as mammographic calcifications or densities.
• The majority are not precursors of cancer.
• These lesions are classified according to the subsequent risk of cancer in
either breast.
• Although risk reduction can be achieved by surgery or chemoprevention, the
majority of affected females will not develop cancer and many undergo
surveillance instead of surgical intervention.
CARCINOMA IN SITU
Carcinoma in situ (literally, “carcinoma in its original place”) refers
to cancer cells confined within ducts and lobules by a basement
membrane. Many (if not all) of the molecular changes found in invasive carcinoma are also found in these lesions; thus, carcinoma in situ
is an apt description.
Ductal and lobular are used to describe subsets of in situ and
invasive carcinoma, but these terms are misleading, as most evidence suggests all breast carcinomas arise from cells in the terminal
duct lobular unit. Carcinoma in situ was originally classified as
ductal or lobular based on the resemblance of the involved spaces to
normal ducts or lobules, but it is now recognized that these growth
patterns are unrelated to the cell of origin and instead reflect differences in tumor cell genetics and biology.
Ductal Carcinoma In Situ
DCIS is a neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells limited to ducts
and lobules by the basement membrane. Myoepithelial cells are
generally preserved in involved ducts/lobules. DCIS can spread
throughout the ductal system and produce extensive lesions involving
an entire segment of the breast.
DCIS is almost always detected by mammography. Most are identified due to associated calcifications; less commonly, periductal fibrosis
surrounding DCIS results in a mammographic density or creates a
vaguely palpable mass. Rarely, DCIS (often of micropapillary or papillary types) can present as nipple discharge or as an incidental finding
upon biopsy for another lesion.
DCIS is separated into low- and high-grade lesions that appear to be
biologically distinct and follow separate pathways of progression to
invasive carcinoma. Low-grade DCIS is typically estrogen receptor
(ER)-positive and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-
negative and has molecular alterations of low-grade breast neoplasia
pathway (discussed later), such as 16q loss and 1q gain. In contrast,
high-grade DCIS may be ER-negative and/or HER2-positive and shows
molecular alterations (genomic instability, chromosomal changes) seen
in high-grade invasive carcinomas.

DCIS grows in several architectural patterns (Fig. 23.12). Its classification is
primarily based on nuclear grade (assessment of nuclear features such as size
and shape). The identification of intraductal calcifications (Fig. 23.12A) is an
important clue to the presence of DCIS; calcifications may be associated with
the presence of central (comedo) necrosis (mostly seen in high-grade DCIS,
Fig. 23.12B) or intraluminal secretions. Cribriform DCIS has rounded (cookie
cutter–like) spaces, often filled with calcified secretory material (Fig. 23.12C).
Micropapillary DCIS produces complex bulbous protrusions without fibrovascular cores (Fig. 23.12D). Papillary DCIS produces true papillae with
fibrovascular cores that lack a myoepithelial cell layer.
Paget disease of the nipple is a rare manifestation of breast cancer (1% to
4% of cases) that presents as a unilateral erythematous eruption with a scale
crust. Pruritus is common and the lesion may be mistaken for eczema. Malignant cells (Paget cells) extend from DCIS within the ductal system via the
lactiferous sinuses into nipple skin without crossing the basement membrane
(Fig. 23.13). The tumor cells disrupt the normal epithelial barrier, allowing
extracellular fluid to seep out onto the nipple surface. Paget cells are readily
detected by nipple biopsy or cytologic preparations of the exudate.

LCIS is a neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells within ducts and
lobules that grow in a dyscohesive fashion. It is almost always an

incidental biopsy finding since it is rarely associated with calcifications
or  stromal  reactions  that  produce  mammographic  densities.  As  a

unchanged by mammographic screening. When both breasts are biop-
sied, LCIS is bilateral in 20% to 40% of cases, as compared with 10% to
20% of cases of DCIS.
The cells of atypical lobular hyperplasia, LCIS, and invasive lobular
carcinoma are morphologically identical. The dyscohesion of the cells
is usually due to loss-of-function of E-cadherin, a transmembrane cell

excision. Other treatment strategies include mastectomy or endocrine
therapy in select cases.

INVASIVE CARCINOMA OF THE BREAST
Breast cancer is the most common malignancy globally and the
leading cause of cancer death in females worldwide. In 2020, breast
cancer surpassed lung cancer as the most common cancer overall with
an estimated 2.3 million new cases, accounting for almost 12% of new
cancer diagnoses across the world. The continued rise in the worldwide incidence of breast cancer is mainly attributable to social and
lifestyle factors; however, improvements in survival outcomes have
been attained, mainly in higher resourced countries, through earlier
diagnosis and the development of more effective adjuvant therapy.
Breast cancer is a heterogenous disease that encompasses numerous tumor subtypes defined by distinct clinical, morphological, and
molecular phenotypes. Several approaches can be used to subclassify
breast cancer into clinically meaningful subgroups (Fig. 23.15). At
diagnosis, morphological assessment delineates in situ from
invasive disease and informs histological tumor type, grade, and
anatomic stage. The routine evaluation of three biomarkers—ER, PR,
and HER2—separates tumors into three major clinical groups, ER-positive/HER2-negative (“luminal”), HER2-positive (“HER2”), and
ER/PR/HER2-negative (triple negative breast cancer, “TNBC”),
which differ with respect to tumor biology, natural history, and
treatment response.
However, characterization of morphology and ER, PR, and HER2
expression do not come close to capturing the full molecular heterogeneity of breast cancer. A useful molecular classification system that better reflects the spectrum of breast cancer biology and behavior separates
breast cancers into six major “intrinsic” subtypes based on gene expression profiling; luminal A, luminal B, HER2 enriched, basal-like, normal-like, and claudin-low. Because these molecular subtypes correlate reasonably well with ER and HER2 protein expression, which is easily
assessed by standard clinical assays, molecular subtyping by expression
profiling is not a routine part of breast cancer classification. However,
gene expression signatures provide predictive and prognostic information and several assays based on gene expression have been developed
that help guide treatment decisions in certain clinical contexts.
Incidence and Epidemiology
The lifetime risk of developing breast cancer is one in eight for
females living to age 90 years in the United States. In 2023, it is
estimated that 297,790 females in the United States will be diagnosed
with invasive breast cancer, and more than 43,000 females will die of
the disease—a toll among cancers second only to lung cancer. Incidence rates vary geographically, with the highest incidence reported
in North America, Northern and Western Europe, and Australia/New
Zealand. However, breast cancer incidence and mortality are increasing at an alarming rate in many low-resource countries. The factors
underlying this trend are thought to be social changes that increase
breast cancer risk—specifically, delayed childbearing, fewer pregnancies, and reduced breastfeeding—combined with late presentation
and a lack of access to optimal health care.
Breast cancer is rare in females younger than age 25 years and
increases in incidence rapidly after age 30 years (Fig. 23.16). While the
incidence of TNBC and HER2 cancer plateaus in middle age (,40 years),
the incidence of luminal cancer continues to rise and peaks later in life.
As a result, TNBCs and HER2 cancers account for almost half of breast
cancers in young females and fewer than 20% of cancers in older females.
The 1980s saw a marked increase in the apparent incidence of
breast cancer in older females due to two factors: (1) the introduction
of mammographic screening, leading to increased cancer detection;
and (2) the increased use of postmenopausal hormonal therapy. After
2000, the number of newly diagnosed breast cancers fell in older females, probably due to a plateauing of the rate of mammographic
screening (approximately 65% to 75% of eligible females) and a decline
in the use of postmenopausal hormone therapy. In contrast, over the
same time the incidence of breast cancer remained relatively constant
in younger females.
Mammography is used to detect nonpalpable asymptomatic breast
carcinomas and is the major screening test for breast cancer. The
principal mammographic signs (none of which are specific) of breast
carcinoma are densities, architectural distortions, and calcifications. The
average size of invasive carcinoma detected by mammography is about
1 cm (significantly smaller than carcinomas detected by palpation). The
sensitivity and specificity of mammography increases with age. At age
40 years, the probability that a mammographic lesion is cancer is only 10%
but this rises to greater than 25% in females older than 50 years. Approximately 10% of invasive carcinomas are not visible on standard, two-dimensional mammographic images. Other imaging modalities, including
digital breast tomosynthesis, ultrasonography, and magnetic resonance
imaging, can be useful adjuncts in such circumstances.

ethnic groups.

gradually declined, most recently by 1% to 2% per year; the current

mortality rate. Although this difference is explained partly by unequal
access to care, breast cancers in females of African descent are also
more likely to be biologically aggressive (e.g., TNBC) and to fall into
molecular subtypes that are difficult to treat.

estimated that around 20% of breast cancers can be attributed to
modifiable risk factors, including obesity, alcohol consumption, and
low physical activity. There is concern (but no proof) that environ-
mental contaminants, such as organochlorine pesticides and certain
plastics, have estrogenic effects on humans that increase the risk of
breast cancer.
The major factors that decrease risk are early pregnancy (prior to
20 years of age) and prolonged breastfeeding. Societal changes in these
factors in low-resource countries are thought to be contributing to
the rise in breast cancer incidence worldwide. Surgical and medical
interventions can decrease risk. Bilateral prophylactic mastectomy de-
creases risk by about 90%. Chemoprevention using ER antagonists
decreases the incidence of ER-positive cancers. These interventions
are mainly offered to females at very high risk for breast cancer (e.g.,
females with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations).
Pathogenesis of Breast Cancer
Like other cancers, breast cancers arise through several pathways
that involve the stepwise acquisition of driver mutations in epithe-
lial cells. The mutation that initiates the process, as demonstrated by
inherited cancers (discussed later), appears to strongly influence the
phenotype of the cancer that ultimately develops, as may the specific
cell type in which the initiating event occurs. Low-grade and high-
grade breast carcinomas differ in their molecular profiles and are
thought  to  evolve  along  largely  separate  pathways  from  distinct
precursor lesions (Fig. 23.17).
The low-grade breast neoplasia pathway proceeds through recog-
nizable ER-positive precursor lesions, including columnar cell lesions,
flat epithelial atypia (i.e., columnar cell lesions with atypia), atypical
hyperplasia (ductal and lobular), low-grade DCIS, and classic LCIS,
which share the potential to progress to low-grade ER-positive inva-
sive carcinoma. At the genetic level, this pathway is defined by specific
genomic alterations, such as loss of 16q and gain of 1q, and a pre-
dominantly “luminal” gene expression signature.
The major precursor lesion of high-grade invasive carcinoma is
high-grade DCIS. The lesions that constitute the earliest steps in
the high-grade breast neoplasia pathway have yet to be identified.
Common alterations associated with the high-grade pathway in-
clude loss of 13q, gain of 11q13, amplification of 17q12, and a gene
expression signature enriched for genes that are highly expressed in
proliferating cells.
As with other carcinomas that begin as in situ lesions, it is not clear
what drives the transition from in situ to invasive breast carcinoma.
Most genomic changes observed in invasive carcinoma are already
present in noninvasive precursor lesions, including major driver muta-
tions. Indeed, genomic changes specific to invasive carcinoma have not
been identified, suggesting that invasion may depend on other factors,
such as changes in the tumor microenvironment, rather than in the
tumor cells.
There is an increasing awareness that the tumor microenvironment
(stromal cells, immune cells, and extracellular matrix) plays an impor-
tant role in breast cancer initiation, progression, and dissemination.
Maintenance of the basement membrane depends on the interaction of
luminal cells, myoepithelial cells, and stromal cells in the local microen-
vironment. In some in situ cancers, myoepithelial cells are reduced in
number and the associated basement membrane is thin and has gaps,
which may set the stage for stromal invasion by breast cancer cells.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts may contribute to tumor progression by
facilitating cell adhesion, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immuno-
suppression. Breast cancer cells can suppress the host immune response
through several mechanisms, including the upregulation of certain cell
surface ligands such as the immune checkpoint protein programmed cell
death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) (Chapter 7). Through these types of dynamic
interactions, cancer cells can create a “tumor promoting” microenviron-
ment that allows them to evade the host immune response.
We now turn to a more in-depth discussion of the major molecular
pathways involved in the pathogenesis of familial and sporadic breast
cancer.
Pathogenesis of Familial Breast Cancer
It is believed that 25% to 35% of breast cancers occur due to the
inheritance of a variant in a susceptibility gene or genes. Single
gene mutations with moderate to high penetrance (“penetrance” re-
fers to the risk of an individual with the mutated gene developing
cancer) accounts for 8% to 17% of breast carcinoma (Table 23.3). In-
heritance is also thought to play a role in an additional 15% to 20% of
females based on a positive family history, defined as breast cancer in
a first-degree relative (mother, sister, or daughter), in multiple rela-
tives, or with onset at an early age. In these females, inheritance of a
single susceptibility gene variant with low penetrance or combina-
tions of polymorphic variants that interact is believed to explain in-
creased risk.
The most important high penetrance susceptibility genes for famil-
ial breast cancer are tumor suppressor genes that regulate genomic
stability or cell growth (Table 23.3). Risk is inherited in an autosomal
dominant fashion and stems from alleles with loss-of-function mutations.

arise via the dominant low-grade ER-positive pathway of breast cancer
development and constitute 50% to 65% of cases. The major risk factor
for luminal breast cancer is estrogen exposure (Table 23.2), which may
promote the development of breast cancer through several mechanisms.
• Estrogen increases the local production of growth factors, such as
transforming growth factor a, platelet-derived growth factor, and
fibroblast growth factor.
• Estrogen regulates the expression of dozens of genes in breast epithelial
cells that may directly contribute to tumor growth and development.
• Estrogen stimulates the proliferation of breast epithelial cells during
puberty, menstrual cycles, and pregnancy, thereby increasing the number of cells that are “at risk” for transformation. The DNA replication
that attends cellular proliferation is conducive to the accumulation
of mutations, and the lull in cell division that occurs during the latter
part of the menstrual cycle may allow time for defective DNA repair
to occur and for mutations to become “fixed” in the genome. Repeti-tion of this process during each cycle may underlie the association
between the cumulative number of menstrual cycles a female experiences and her risk of developing breast cancer, as well as the strong
association between luminal cancers and age (Fig. 23.16).
Clear evidence of the importance of estrogen is found in the therapeutic benefits of estrogen antagonists, which reduce the development
of luminal cancers in females at high risk, and the increased incidence
of luminal cancers in females treated with postmenopausal hormone

Fig. 23.18 Molecular classification of invasive breast cancer. Three major groups of breast cancer are distinguished
by characteristic changes in DNA, mRNA, protein, and morphology. Genomic abnormalities are shown in Circos
plots (Chapter 7), which present a snapshot of all the genomic abnormalities within a particular tumor; these abnormalities
are mapped onto the chromosomes, which are displayed at the periphery of a circle. Green loops show
intrachromosomal rearrangements, while red loops show interchromosomal rearrangements. Gene expression
(mRNA) profiling measures relative levels of mRNA expression. Red indicates a relative increase; green, a relative
decrease; and black, no change in levels. Genes are arrayed from top to bottom and tumors from left to right. Immunohistochemical
studies detect proteins using specific antibodies visualized with a brown chromogen. Luminal
(ER-positive/HER2-negative) cancers are diverse, ranging from well-differentiated cancers with low proliferative
rates and few chromosomal changes to poorly differentiated cancers with high proliferative rates and large numbers
of chromosomal rearrangements. All of these cancers express ER (an estrogen-dependent transcription factor).
Proliferation is estimated by counting mitoses or by staining for proliferation markers such as Ki-67 . HER2-
positive cancers may be ER-positive or ER-negative, but when ER is present, levels are typically low. HER2
positivity can be detected as an increase in HER2 gene copy number, an increase in HER2 mRNA, or an increase
in HER2 protein, as shown here. Triple negative breast cancers (ER-negative/HER2-negative; this group largely
overlaps with “basal-like” carcinomas defined by mRNA expression) are characterized by genomic instability (denoted
by numerous chromosomal changes), a high proliferative rate, and expression of many proteins typical of
myoepithelial cells (e.g., basal keratins). ER, Estrogen receptor; HER2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2.

Fig. 23.18 Molecular classification of invasive breast cancer. Three major groups of breast cancer are distinguished by characteristic changes in DNA, mRNA, protein, and morphology. Genomic abnormalities are shown in Circos plots (Chapter 7), which present a snapshot of all the genomic abnormalities within a particular tumor; these abnormalities are mapped onto the chromosomes, which are displayed at the periphery of a circle. Green loops show intrachromosomal rearrangements, while red loops show interchromosomal rearrangements. Gene expression (mRNA) profiling measures relative levels of mRNA expression. Red indicates a relative increase; green, a relative decrease; and black, no change in levels. Genes are arrayed from top to bottom and tumors from left to right. Immunohistochemical studies detect proteins using specific antibodies visualized with a brown chromogen. Luminal (ER-positive/HER2-negative) cancers are diverse, ranging from well-differentiated cancers with low proliferative rates and few chromosomal changes to poorly differentiated cancers with high proliferative rates and large numbers of chromosomal rearrangements. All of these cancers express ER (an estrogen-dependent transcription factor). Proliferation is estimated by counting mitoses or by staining for proliferation markers such as Ki-67. HER2- positive cancers may be ER-positive or ER-negative, but when ER is present, levels are typically low. HER2 positivity can be detected as an increase in HER2 gene copy number, an increase in HER2 mRNA, or an increase in HER2 protein, as shown here. Triple negative breast cancers (ER-negative/HER2-negative; this group largely overlaps with “basal-like” carcinomas defined by mRNA expression) are characterized by genomic instability (denoted by numerous chromosomal changes), a high proliferative rate, and expression of many proteins typical of myoepithelial cells (e.g., basal keratins). ER, Estrogen receptor; HER2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2.

ER, Estrogen receptor; HER2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2; mRNA, messenger RNA; TNBC, triple negative breast cancer; NST, no special type.
lower ER and PR protein expression, have a higher proliferation
rate, tend to have a greater burden of chromosomal aberrations,
and are more aggressive than luminal A cancers. They sometimes
arise from luminal A cancers following the acquisition of mutations
in genes that regulate genomic stability, such as TP53, and frequently occur in patients with germline BRCA2 mutations.
Several special histologic subtypes (described later), including lobular,
tubular, cribriform and mucinous carcinomas, are also typically “luminal.”
HER2-Positive Cancers. HER2 cancers arise through a pathway
that is strongly associated with amplification of the HER2 gene
on chromosome 17q. Cancers with HER2 amplification constitute
approximately 20% of all breast cancers and may be either ER-positive
or ER-negative. HER2 (also known as ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine
kinase that promotes cell proliferation and opposes apoptosis by stimulating the RAS and PI3K-AKT signaling pathways. The only common
molecular mechanism for HER2 overexpression is HER2 gene amplification, found in .95% of HER2-positive carcinomas. In addition,
these cancers characteristically have complex interchromosomal rearrangements and a high burden of mutations, which often involve TP53
and PIK3CA. This is the most common subtype of breast cancer in patients with germline TP53 mutations (Li-Fraumeni syndrome).
HER2 cancers are typically high-grade (Table 23.4), growing in
solid sheets comprised of highly proliferative pleomorphic tumor cells.
Apocrine carcinoma is a special histologic subtype that is frequently
HER2-positive. Clinically, HER2 carcinomas are diagnosed by detecting HER2 protein overexpression by immunohistochemistry or HER2
gene amplification by in situ hybridization (Fig. 23.19).
Triple Negative Breast Cancers. TNBCs arise through an estrogen-independent pathway that is not associated with HER2 gene amplification. They account for about 15% of breast cancers and are a heterogenous
group of tumors with distinct molecular drivers and clinicopathological
phenotypes. The majority of TNBCs have a “basal-like” gene expression
profile, so-called because many genes that comprise this signature are
normally expressed in basally located myoepithelial cells.
As a group, high-grade TNBCs are characterized by marked
genomic instability due to defects in DNA repair by homologous
recombination that manifests as complex copy number alterations
and chromosomal rearrangements. In familial breast cancer, defective
homologous recombination is often caused by BRCA1 and BRCA2

Most breast malignancies are adenocarcinomas, which are subdivided into around 20 subtypes based on morphological appearances.
The most common is invasive breast carcinoma of “no special type”,
which accounts for approximately 75% of invasive breast carcinomas.
This heterogenous group of tumors is segregated from those belonging to “special” histologic types with distinct morphologic features,
such as unique patterns of growth, tumor architecture, and cytomorphology.
We will first cover the morphologic features of invasive carcinomas of no special type and will then discuss several special subtypes
of invasive carcinoma with informative pathogenic and clinical
associations.
MORPHOLOGY
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type. In the absence of mammographic screening, these carcinomas usually present as a mass of at least 2 to
3 cm in size. The mammographic and gross appearance varies widely depending
on the stromal reaction to the tumor (Fig. 23.20). They most commonly present as
a hard, irregular, radiodense mass (Fig. 23.20A and B) associated with a desmoplastic stromal reaction (Fig. 23.20C). When cut or scraped, such tumors typically produce a characteristic grating sound due to areas of chalky-white desmoplastic stroma and occasional foci of calcification. Less commonly, tumors present
as a deceptively well-circumscribed mass composed of sheets of tumor cells with
scant stromal reaction or alternatively may be almost imperceptible, being comprised of scattered neoplastic glands or single tumor cells infiltrating otherwise
unremarkable fibrofatty tissue. Some invasive carcinomas of no special type are
high-grade tumors with prominent populations of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs). These were previously considered a special subtype referred to as
medullary carcinoma; however, this entity did not prove to be diagnostically reproducible, and such tumors are diagnosed in the current classification system as
invasive carcinoma of no special type with “medullary pattern”.
Histologic grading. Grade refers to how closely the tumor resembles the
normal structure of the breast (i.e., differentiation). All invasive carcinomas are
graded using the Nottingham Histologic Score based on the degree of glandular differentiation (tubule formation), nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic rate.
Grade 1 (well differentiated) carcinomas grow in a tubular or cribriform pattern
and have small uniform nuclei and a low proliferative rate (Fig. 23.21A and D).
Grade 2 (moderately differentiated) carcinomas have areas where cells grow
as solid clusters or single infiltrating cells and show greater nuclear pleomorphism and higher numbers of mitotic figures (Fig. 23.21B and E). Grade 3
(poorly differentiated) carcinomas invade as ragged nests or solid sheets of
cells and have enlarged irregular nuclei. A high proliferative rate and areas of
tumor necrosis are common in high-grade tumors (Fig. 23.21C and F).

MORPHOLOGY
Some special histologic subtypes of breast cancer almost always fall
within the luminal (ER-positive/HER2-negative) group. These include inva-
sive lobular carcinoma, mucinous carcinoma, tubular carcinoma, cribriform carci-
noma, and papillary carcinoma. Invasive lobular carcinoma often infiltrates
the breast insidiously while producing minimal desmoplasia, making it difficult to
detect on imaging studies. The histologic hallmark is the presence of dyscohe-
sive infiltrating tumor cells arranged in linear cords, often including signet ring
cells  containing  intracytoplasmic  mucin  (Fig.  23.22A).  Mucinous  (colloid)
carcinoma is soft or rubbery and gelatinous with pushing or circumscribed
borders. The tumor cells are arranged in clusters of varying size within large
lakes of mucin (Fig. 23.22B). Tubular carcinoma consists exclusively of well-
formed  tubules  and  is  sometimes  mistaken  for  a  benign  sclerosing  lesion
(Fig. 23.22C). Cribriform carcinoma consists of invasive nests with cribriform
morphology. Papillary carcinoma produces true papillary fronds lined by tumor
cells (Fig. 23.22D).

The tumor cells of apocrine carcinoma resemble the cells that line sweat

within intercellular fluid, creating structures that mimic the appearance of papil-

TNBC (ER/PR/HER2-negative)  carcinomas often belong to one  of
several special histologic types. Carcinomas demonstrating squamous or
mesenchymal (e.g., spindle, chondroid, osseous) differentiation are termed
metaplastic carcinoma (Fig.23.22G) These carcinomas often have gene ex-
pression profiles resembling those of myoepithelial cells and typically have a
poor prognosis. However, rare indolent subtypes of metaplastic carcinoma are
also  recognized,  including  low-grade  adenosquamous  carcinoma  and

cinoma,  mucoepidermoid  carcinoma,  and  secretory  carcinoma
(Fig. 23.22H); these are collectively referred to as salivary gland-like carcino-
mas because they are identical to their more common counterparts in the

Inflammatory breast carcinoma is not a special histologic type but refers
instead to a distinct clinical presentation caused by extensive plugging of the
lymphovascular spaces of the dermis by carcinoma cells that leads to diffuse
breast erythema, swelling, and skin thickening. The edematous skin is tethered
to the breast by Cooper ligaments, producing skin dimpling that mimics the
surface of an orange peel, an appearance referred to as peau d’orange. The
presentation can be confused with infection, leading to delayed diagnosis;
however, the name “inflammatory” is a misnomer, as typically no inflammation
is present. The underlying carcinoma does not typically form a discrete palpa-
ble mass and is usually high-grade and diffusely infiltrative.

964 CHAPTER 23  The Breast
Clinical Presentation
Most invasive breast carcinomas present as a breast mass, detected either
by palpation or mammographic screening. The mode of detection varies
according to molecular subtype (Table 23.4). Cancers detected by mam-
mographic screening are usually small luminal cancers limited to the
breast, while HER2 positive cancers and TNBCs are aggressive and more
likely to be detected as palpable masses. Larger carcinomas may invade the
pectoralis muscle and become fixed to the chest wall or invade the dermis
and cause retraction (dimpling) of the skin. When the tumor involves the
central breast, retraction of the nipple may develop. Rarely, breast cancer
presents as metastasis to an axillary lymph node or a distant site before
cancer is detected in the breast. In such cases, the primary carcinoma may
be small, obscured by dense breast tissue, or fail to produce a desmoplastic
response. In most cases, these “occult” primary tumors (which are easily
missed by palpation or mammography) are detected by imaging studies
using ultrasound or MRI.
Prognostic and Predictive Factors
The outcome for females with breast cancer depends on the biologic
features of the carcinoma (the molecular or histologic type) and the
stage of disease at the time of diagnosis. Based on these factors, some
females with breast cancer have a normal life expectancy, whereas others
have only a 10% chance of being alive in 5 years. Patients who present
at an advanced stage with distant metastasis (5% of patients) or with
inflammatory carcinoma (1% to 5% of patients) have a particularly poor
prognosis. For other cancers, prognosis is determined by pathologic
evaluation of the primary tumor and the axillary lymph nodes, as well as
the biomarker expression profile (Table 23.5).
Prognostic  factors  are  important  in  counseling  patients  about
the likely outcome of their disease, choosing the most appropriate
treatment, and designing clinical trials. Predictive factors help to deter-
mine the likely response of a cancer to a specific type of treatment.
Factors related to tumor biology are usually both prognostic and pre-
dictive (e.g., ER and HER2 expression, proliferation), whereas factors
related to tumor extent (e.g., tumor size, lymph node metastases, dis-
tant metastases) are primarily prognostic.
The major prognostic factors are (Table 23.5):
•  Distant metastases. Distant metastatic spread is the most important
prognostic factor for invasive carcinoma. Once distant metastases are
present, cure is unlikely, although long-term remissions and pallia-
tion can be achieved, especially in females with ER-positive and
HER2-positive tumors.
•  Lymph node metastases. Axillary lymph node status is the most im-
portant prognostic factor for invasive carcinoma in the absence of
distant metastases. The clinical assessment of lymph node status is
unreliable due to both false-positives (e.g., palpable reactive nodes)
and false-negatives (e.g., lymph nodes with small metastatic depos-
its). Therefore, histological examination is necessary for accurate
assessment. With no nodal involvement, the 10-year disease-free
survival rate is 70% to 80%; the rate falls to 35% to 40% with one to
three positive nodes and to 10% to 15% when more than 10 nodes
are positive.
Lymphatic vessels in most breast carcinomas drain first to one
or two sentinel nodes, which can be identified with radiotracer or
colored dyes. If a biopsy of sentinel nodes is negative for metastasis,
it is unlikely that other, more distant nodes will be involved; this ap-
proach is used to spare patients the morbidity of complete axillary
dissection. Approximately 10% to 20% of females without axillary
lymph node metastases experience recurrence with distant metasta-
sis. In these patients, metastasis may occur via the internal mam-
mary lymph nodes or hematogenously.

Carcinoma
AJCC, American Joint Committee on Cancer; ER, estrogen receptor; HER2,
human epidermal growth factor receptor 2; PR, progesterone receptor;
TNBC, triple negative breast cancer.
•  Tumor size. Females with node-negative carcinoma less than 1 cm in
size have a 10-year survival rate of more than 90%, whereas survival
drops to 77% for cancers greater than 2 cm.
•  Locally advanced disease. Carcinomas invading the skin or skeletal
muscle are usually large, making it difficult to achieve local control.
•  Histologic grade. Within each of the tumor staging groups, high-
grade invasive carcinomas have a worse prognosis than low-grade
tumors. Given the strength of this association, histologic grade is
now incorporated as a modifying factor in the “prognostic staging
system” (see later).
•  Histologic subtype. Several histologic subtypes of invasive carcinoma
have prognostic implications. These include tubular and cribriform
carcinomas, which are always associated with a good prognosis;
and metaplastic carcinoma, which is divided into several histologic
subtypes that are variously associated with good or poor clinical
outcomes. Tumor type also influences patient management and can
predict therapeutic outcome (e.g., invasive lobular carcinoma and
metaplastic carcinoma are less responsive to neoadjuvant chemo-
therapy than invasive carcinoma of no special type).
•  Lymphovascular  invasion.  Tumor  cells  are  seen  within  vascular
spaces (either lymphatics or small capillaries) in about half of all
invasive carcinomas. This is a poor prognostic factor for overall
survival in females without lymph node metastases and is associated
with a higher risk of local recurrence.

Factors related to tumor biology are usually both prognostic and predictive (e.g., ER and HER2 expression, proliferation), whereas factors related to tumor extent (e.g., tumor size, lymph node metastases, distant metastases) are primarily prognostic.

Clinical Presentation

Most invasive breast carcinomas present as a breast mass, detected either by palpation or mammographic screening. The mode of detection varies according to molecular subtype (Table 23.4). Cancers detected by mammographic screening are usually small luminal cancers limited to the breast, while HER2 positive cancers and TNBCs are aggressive and more likely to be detected as palpable masses. Larger carcinomas may invade the pectoralis muscle and become fixed to the chest wall or invade the dermis and cause retraction (dimpling) of the skin. When the tumor involves the central breast, retraction of the nipple may develop. Rarely, breast cancer presents as metastasis to an axillary lymph node or a distant site before cancer is detected in the breast. In such cases, the primary carcinoma may be small, obscured by dense breast tissue, or fail to produce a desmoplastic response. In most cases, these “occult” primary tumors (which are easily missed by palpation or mammography) are detected by imaging studies using ultrasound or MRI.
Prognostic and Predictive Factors

The outcome for females with breast cancer depends on the biologic features of the carcinoma (the molecular or histologic type) and the stage of disease at the time of diagnosis. Based on these factors, some females with breast cancer have a normal life expectancy, whereas others have only a 10% chance of being alive in 5 years. Patients who present at an advanced stage with distant metastasis (5% of patients) or with inflammatory carcinoma (1% to 5% of patients) have a particularly poor prognosis. For other cancers, prognosis is determined by pathologic evaluation of the primary tumor and the axillary lymph nodes, as well as the biomarker expression profile (Table 23.5).

Prognostic  factors  are  important  in  counseling  patients  about the likely outcome of their disease, choosing the most appropriate treatment, and designing clinical trials. Predictive factors help to determine the likely response of a cancer to a specific type of treatment.

Factors related to tumor biology are usually both prognostic and predictive (e.g., ER and HER2 expression, proliferation), whereas factors related to tumor extent (e.g., tumor size, lymph node metastases, distant metastases) are primarily prognostic.
The major prognostic factors are (Table 23.5):

•  Distant metastases. Distant metastatic spread is the most important prognostic factor for invasive carcinoma. Once distant metastases are present, cure is unlikely, although long-term remissions and pallia-tion can be achieved, especially in females with ER-positive and HER2-positive tumors.

•  Lymph node metastases. Axillary lymph node status is the most important prognostic factor for invasive carcinoma in the absence of distant metastases. The clinical assessment of lymph node status is unreliable due to both false-positives (e.g., palpable reactive nodes) and false-negatives (e.g., lymph nodes with small metastatic deposits). Therefore, histological examination is necessary for accurate assessment. With no nodal involvement, the 10-year disease-free survival rate is 70% to 80%; the rate falls to 35% to 40% with one to three positive nodes and to 10% to 15% when more than 10 nodes are positive.

Lymphatic vessels in most breast carcinomas drain first to one or two sentinel nodes, which can be identified with radiotracer or colored dyes. If a biopsy of sentinel nodes is negative for metastasis, it is unlikely that other, more distant nodes will be involved; this approach is used to spare patients the morbidity of complete axillary dissection. Approximately 10% to 20% of females without axillary lymph node metastases experience recurrence with distant metastasis. In these patients, metastasis may occur via the internal mammary lymph nodes or hematogenously.

•  Tumor size. Females with node-negative carcinoma less than 1 cm in size have a 10-year survival rate of more than 90%, whereas survival drops to 77% for cancers greater than 2 cm.
•  Locally advanced disease. Carcinomas invading the skin or skeletal muscle are usually large, making it difficult to achieve local control.

•  Histologic grade. Within each of the tumor staging groups, high-grade invasive carcinomas have a worse prognosis than low-grade tumors. Given the strength of this association, histologic grade is now incorporated as a modifying factor in the “prognostic staging system” (see later).

•  Histologic subtype. Several histologic subtypes of invasive carcinoma have prognostic implications. These include tubular and cribriform carcinomas, which are always associated with a good prognosis; and metaplastic carcinoma, which is divided into several histologic subtypes that are variously associated with good or poor clinical outcomes. Tumor type also influences patient management and can predict therapeutic outcome (e.g., invasive lobular carcinoma and metaplastic carcinoma are less responsive to neoadjuvant chemotherapy than invasive carcinoma of no special type).

•  Lymphovascular  invasion.  Tumor  cells  are  seen  within  vascular spaces (either lymphatics or small capillaries) in about half of all invasive carcinomas. CHAPTER 23 The Breast 965
• Inflammatory carcinoma. As already discussed, inflammatory carcinoma is caused by extensive invasion of dermal lymphovascular channels and portends a poor outcome. The 3-year survival rate is only 3%
to 10%. Only 1% to 5% of cancers are in this group, but the incidence
is higher in females of African descent and younger females.
Additional major prognostic and predictive factors are related to
tumor biology, molecular subtype, and response to therapy (Table 23.5):
• ER. ER is both a prognostic and predictive biomarker. ER-positive
tumors (defined as $1% of tumor cells showing nuclear expression)
respond to endocrine therapies, which reduce the rate of recurrence
and improve survival outcomes. “Low positive” tumors (1% to 10%
ER staining) appear to have a worse prognosis than tumors demonstrating high levels of ER expression.
• PR. Breast cancers that are ER-positive are also typically PR-positive
(defined as $1% of tumor cells showing nuclear expression). However,
ER-positive tumors that show low levels of PR expression have worse
clinical outcomes than tumors with high levels of both ER and PR.
• HER2. HER2 is both a prognostic and predictive biomarker. HER2-
positivity is an indicator of aggressive clinical behavior and
response to HER2-targeting agents.
• Gene expression profiling. Several proprietary assays that quantify
mRNA levels in breast cancer cells have been developed. Most are
heavily weighted toward inclusion of genes that are involved in
proliferation. The greatest clinical value of these assays is to identify
patients with slow-growing, ER-positive cancers who can be spared
the toxicity of chemotherapy.
• Response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Treating patients prior to
surgery provides the opportunity to observe the tumor response to
chemotherapy. One-third or more of TNBCs and HER2 cancers
regress completely (termed “pathologic complete response”) following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Patients with responsive cancers
belonging to these subtypes have a better prognosis than patients
with nonresponsive cancers.
• Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. TILs are mononuclear immune cells
(lymphocytes and plasma cells) infiltrating the tumor and its
stroma. A prominent TIL component is associated with improved
prognosis and better response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in
HER2 and TNBC.
• ESR1. Mutations in ESR1 (the gene that encodes ER) are major
drivers of endocrine therapy resistance in ER-positive metastatic
breast cancer, resulting in constitutive activation of ER and a
worse prognosis. Testing for ESR1 mutations is recommended for
ER-positive/HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer at the time of
recurrence or progression on endocrine therapy to guide therapeutic decision making.
• Predictive biomarkers for targeted therapies. Several biomarkers
predict response to specific classes of drugs. Examples include the
response to PARP inhibitors, which is predicted by the presence of
germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations; the response of ER-positive/
HER2-negative breast cancer to PI3K inhibitors, which is predicted
by the presence of PIK3CA mutations; and response of secretory
breast carcinoma to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which is predicted
by the presence NTRK gene fusions. Similarly, response of breast
carcinoma to specific immune checkpoint inhibitors is correlated
with expression of PD-L1 in tumor and immune cells, tumor mutational burden (as assessed by NextGen sequencing), and the presence of mismatch repair deficiency (which is rare in breast cancer).
• Circulating tumor DNA. Sequencing fragmented tumor-derived
DNA shed into the blood by nonviable cancer cells can detect
emerging actionable mutations for targeted therapy (e.g., PIK3CA
mutations).
Breast Cancer Staging
The most important prognostic factors are included in the latest American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, which integrates the anatomic stage and the molecular characteristics of individual breast cancers (Table 23.6). The anatomic stage (0 to IV) considers
the primary tumor (T), involvement of regional lymph nodes (N), and
the presence of distant metastases (M). The prognostic stage then takes
into consideration histologic grade and biologic features (e.g., ER, PR,
and HER2 status, as well as multigene panel results, if available) to ad-just the disease stage, with the aim of improving prognostic accuracy.
For example, in some cases TNBC is “up-staged” in the new prognostic
staging system to reflect its more aggressive behavior, while most luminal cancers are “down-staged.” The TNM staging system also considers
clinical features that are associated with a worse prognosis, including
inflammatory carcinoma, skin ulceration, and chest wall infiltration.
Management of Breast Cancer
The main goals of breast cancer therapy are to control local disease and
to prolong survival by treating known or potential distant metastases.
Local control is achieved in most patients with breast-conserving surgery
and radiation therapy. Mastectomy is generally only necessary for locally

• Inflammatory carcinoma. As already discussed, inflammatory carcinoma is caused by extensive invasion of dermal lymphovascular channels and portends a poor outcome. The 3-year survival rate is only 3% to 10%. Only 1% to 5% of cancers are in this group, but the incidence is higher in females of African descent and younger females. Additional major prognostic and predictive factors are related to tumor biology, molecular subtype, and response to therapy (Table 23.5):

• ER. ER is both a prognostic and predictive biomarker. ER-positive tumors (defined as $1% of tumor cells showing nuclear expression) respond to endocrine therapies, which reduce the rate of recurrence and improve survival outcomes. “Low positive” tumors (1% to 10% ER staining) appear to have a worse prognosis than tumors demonstrating high levels of ER expression.

• PR. Breast cancers that are ER-positive are also typically PR-positive (defined as $1% of tumor cells showing nuclear expression). However, ER-positive tumors that show low levels of PR expression have worse clinical outcomes than tumors with high levels of both ER and PR.
• HER2. HER2 is both a prognostic and predictive biomarker. HER2- positivity is an indicator of aggressive clinical behavior and response to HER2-targeting agents.

• Gene expression profiling. Several proprietary assays that quantify mRNA levels in breast cancer cells have been developed. Most are heavily weighted toward inclusion of genes that are involved in proliferation. The greatest clinical value of these assays is to identify patients with slow-growing, ER-positive cancers who can be spared the toxicity of chemotherapy.

• Response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Treating patients prior to surgery provides the opportunity to observe the tumor response to chemotherapy. One-third or more of TNBCs and HER2 cancers regress completely (termed “pathologic complete response”) following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Patients with responsive cancers belonging to these subtypes have a better prognosis than patients with nonresponsive cancers.

• Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. TILs are mononuclear immune cells (lymphocytes and plasma cells) infiltrating the tumor and its stroma. A prominent TIL component is associated with improved prognosis and better response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in HER2 and TNBC.

• ESR1. Mutations in ESR1 (the gene that encodes ER) are major drivers of endocrine therapy resistance in ER-positive metastatic breast cancer, resulting in constitutive activation of ER and a worse prognosis. Testing for ESR1 mutations is recommended for ER-positive/HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer at the time of recurrence or progression on endocrine therapy to guide therapeutic decision making.

• Predictive biomarkers for targeted therapies. Several biomarkers predict response to specific classes of drugs. Examples include the response to PARP inhibitors, which is predicted by the presence of germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations; the response of ER-positive/ HER2-negative breast cancer to PI3K inhibitors, which is predicted by the presence of PIK3CA mutations; and response of secretory breast carcinoma to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which is predicted by the presence NTRK gene fusions. Similarly, response of breast carcinoma to specific immune checkpoint inhibitors is correlated with expression of PD-L1 in tumor and immune cells, tumor mutational burden (as assessed by NextGen sequencing), and the presence of mismatch repair deficiency (which is rare in breast cancer).
• Circulating tumor DNA. Sequencing fragmented tumor-derived DNA shed into the blood by nonviable cancer cells can detect emerging actionable mutations for targeted therapy (e.g., PIK3CA mutations).
Breast Cancer Staging

The most important prognostic factors are included in the latest American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, which integrates the anatomic stage and the molecular characteristics of individual breast cancers (Table 23.6). The anatomic stage (0 to IV) considers the primary tumor (T), involvement of regional lymph nodes (N), and the presence of distant metastases (M). The prognostic stage then takes into consideration histologic grade and biologic features (e.g., ER, PR, and HER2 status, as well as multigene panel results, if available) to ad-just the disease stage, with the aim of improving prognostic accuracy. For example, in some cases TNBC is “up-staged” in the new prognostic staging system to reflect its more aggressive behavior, while most luminal cancers are “down-staged.” The TNM staging system also considers clinical features that are associated with a worse prognosis, including inflammatory carcinoma, skin ulceration, and chest wall infiltration. KEY CONCEPTS
Invasive Carcinoma of the Breast
•  Breast cancer is the most common nonskin malignancy in females and the
second most common cause of cancer deaths in the United States.
•  The most important risk factors for sporadic cancers in females are estrogenic
stimulation and increasing age.
•  Approximately one-quarter to one-third of breast cancers are familial,
being related to inheritance of genetic variants that increase breast
cancer risk.
•  High-risk genes associated with familial breast cancer include several in-
volved with DNA repair and genomic stability, most notably BRCA1, BRCA2,
PALB2, and TP53.
•  The most common histologic subtype is invasive breast carcinoma of no
special type, which accounts for around 75% of cases, while invasive lobular
carcinoma is the most common special subtype.
•  Special histologic subtypes have prognostic importance and provide addi-
tional clues linking biologic changes to clinical behavior.
•  Breast cancers cluster into three major molecular groups, luminal (ER-positive),
HER2, and TNBC, each with distinctive biologic and clinical features.
•  Luminal cancers are further divided into two groups, A and B, that differ
mainly in terms of proliferation, which is low in group A and high in group B.
•  HER2 cancers are defined by overexpression of the HER2 receptor, usually
due to HER2 gene amplification, and respond well to HER2 inhibitors.
•  TNBCs lack ER, PR, and HER2 expression, are often associated with defects
in DNA repair and genomic stability (e.g., due to silencing of BRCA1 or TP53
mutation), and carry a relatively poor prognosis.
•  Prognosis is dependent on both biologic features and the extent of cancer
at the time of diagnosis (anatomic stage).
•  In the AJCC eighth edition staging system, molecular group and anatomic
stage are combined to create prognostic stage groups that provide better
estimates of likely survival.
•  Effective treatment requires both local and systemic control of disease.
•  Improvements in treatment are being made as new targeted therapies
are being developed and response to treatment is better understood.
STROMAL TUMORS
The two types of stroma in the breast, intralobular and interlobular,
give rise to distinct types of neoplasms. Two closely related breast-
specific tumors, fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor, arise from cells of
the intralobular stroma. These tumors are termed “biphasic” because
they also include a nonneoplastic epithelial component, the prolifera-
tion of which may be stimulated by growth factors elaborated by the
stromal cells. By contrast, interlobular stroma is a source of the same
types of mesenchymal tumors that occur in connective tissue else-
where in the body (e.g., lipomas and angiosarcomas) as well as a few
unusual stromal tumors that arise more commonly in the breast (e.g.,
myofibroblastoma).

female breast. Two-thirds of fibroadenomas harbor driver mutations in
MED12, a gene that encodes a subunit of the mediator complex, which
is involved in regulating the transcription of RNA polymerase II-depen-
dent genes. The other tumor that is strongly associated with MED12
mutations, uterine leiomyoma, also arises from stromal cells within an
organ that is responsive to female sex hormones. Perhaps by deranging

bilateral  fibroadenomas  that  regress  after  cessation  of  treatment.

Phyllodes Tumor
Phyllodes tumor, like fibroadenoma, arises from intralobular stroma
but is much less common, accounting for approximately 2.5% of fi-
broepithelial lesions. Like fibroadenomas, the majority of phyllodes
tumors have mutations in MED12 (part of the transcriptional regula-
tor mediator complex) and RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha, also
involved in transcriptional regulation), suggesting a shared pathogen-
esis. However, phyllodes tumors are more likely to have mutations in
additional genes such as TERT (the gene that encodes telomerase),
TP53, and RB.
