Most phyllodes tumors are detected as palpable masses, others by mammog-
raphy. The tumors vary in size from a few centimeters to massive lesions
involving the entire breast. The larger lesions often have bulbous protrusions
(phyllodes is Greek for “leaf-like”) due to the presence of nodules of proliferat-
ing stroma covered by epithelium (Fig. 23.25A–B). In some tumors these protru-
sions extend into a cystic space. This growth pattern may also occasionally be
seen in large fibroadenomas and is not an indication of malignancy. Phyllodes
tumors are classified as benign, borderline, or malignant based on the histo-
logic features of the stroma. Benign phyllodes tumors resemble fibroadeno-
mas but their stroma is more cellular and mitotically active. Borderline
phyllodes tumors demonstrate more prominent stromal atypia, cellularity,
and mitotic activity compared to benign phyllodes tumors. Malignant phyl-
lodes tumors are widely infiltrative and may be difficult to distinguish from
sarcoma, particularly when there is marked stromal overgrowth with few re-
sidual epithelial elements.
Clinical Features
Most phyllodes tumors present in the sixth decade, 10 to 20 years later
than the peak age for fibroadenoma. Up to 75% have benign cytologic
features; these occasionally recur locally but do not metastasize. In con-
trast, borderline and malignant phyllodes tumors show an increased rate
of recurrence, with margin status being the most important predictor of
local  recurrence  following  excision.  Regardless  of  grade,  lymphatic
spread is rare, and axillary lymph node dissection is contraindicated.
The uncommon malignant lesions give rise to distant hematogenous
metastases in about one-third of cases. Only the neoplastic stromal
component is present in metastases.
Lesions of Interlobular Stroma
Tumors of the interlobular stroma of the breast are composed of stromal
cells without an accompanying epithelial component. These include be-
nign as well as malignant tumors, all uncommon and hence considered
briefly.
Benign Lesions of Interlobular Stroma
Myofibroblastoma consists of myofibroblasts and is unusual in that it is
the only breast tumor that is equally common in males. Lipomas are
often palpable and can also be detected mammographically as fat-
containing lesions. Fibromatosis is a clonal proliferation of fibroblasts
and myofibroblasts. It presents as an irregular, infiltrating mass that can
involve muscle. Though locally aggressive, this lesion does not metas-
tasize. Some cases are associated with prior trauma or surgery. Other
cases  occur  as  part  of  familial  adenomatous  polyposis,  hereditary
desmoid syndrome, and Gardner syndrome.
Malignant Lesions of Interlobular Stroma
Malignant stromal tumors of the breast are rare. The only sarcoma that
occurs with any frequency in the breast is angiosarcoma; however, it
accounts for less than 0.05% of breast malignancies. Angiosarcoma of
the breast may be sporadic (primary) or arise as a complication of
therapy (secondary). Most sporadic angiosarcomas occur in the breast
parenchyma of young females (mean age 35 years) and have a poor
prognosis. Tumors occurring after treatment for breast cancer typically
arise in older females and are associated with radiation therapy or
chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome). After radiation ther-
apy, approximately 0.3% of females develop angiosarcomas in breast
skin, with most cases being diagnosed 5 to 10 years after treatment. The
molecular hallmark of secondary angiosarcoma is high-level MYC am-

Phyllodes tumor, like fibroadenoma, arises from intralobular stroma but is much less common, accounting for approximately 2.5% of fibroepithelial lesions. Like fibroadenomas, the majority of phyllodes tumors have mutations in MED12 (part of the transcriptional regulator mediator complex) and RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha, also involved in transcriptional regulation), suggesting a shared pathogenesis. However, phyllodes tumors are more likely to have mutations in additional genes such as TERT (the gene that encodes telomerase), TP53, and RB.

MORPHOLOGY

Most phyllodes tumors are detected as palpable masses, others by mammography. The tumors vary in size from a few centimeters to massive lesions involving the entire breast. The larger lesions often have bulbous protrusions

(phyllodes is Greek for “leaf-like”) due to the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (Fig. 23.25A–B). In some tumors these protrusions extend into a cystic space. This growth pattern may also occasionally be

seen in large fibroadenomas and is not an indication of malignancy. Phyllodes

tumors are classified as benign, borderline, or malignant based on the histologic features of the stroma. Benign phyllodes tumors resemble fibroadenomas but their stroma is more cellular and mitotically active. Borderline

phyllodes tumors demonstrate more prominent stromal atypia, cellularity, and mitotic activity compared to benign phyllodes tumors. Malignant phyllodes tumors are widely infiltrative and may be difficult to distinguish from sarcoma, particularly when there is marked stromal overgrowth with few residual epithelial elements.

Clinical Features

Most phyllodes tumors present in the sixth decade, 10 to 20 years later than the peak age for fibroadenoma. Up to 75% have benign cytologic features; these occasionally recur locally but do not metastasize. In contrast, borderline and malignant phyllodes tumors show an increased rate of recurrence, with margin status being the most important predictor of local recurrence following excision. Regardless of grade, lymphatic spread is rare, and axillary lymph node dissection is contraindicated.

The uncommon malignant lesions give rise to distant hematogenous metastases in about one-third of cases. Only the neoplastic stromal component is present in metastases.

Lesions of Interlobular Stroma

Tumors of the interlobular stroma of the breast are composed of stromal cells without an accompanying epithelial component. These include benign as well as malignant tumors, all uncommon and hence considered briefly.

Benign Lesions of Interlobular Stroma

Myofibroblastoma consists of myofibroblasts and is unusual in that it is the only breast tumor that is equally common in males. Lipomas are often palpable and can also be detected mammographically as fat-containing lesions. Fibromatosis is a clonal proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. It presents as an irregular, infiltrating mass that can involve muscle. Though locally aggressive, this lesion does not metastasize. Some cases are associated with prior trauma or surgery. Other cases occur as part of familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary desmoid syndrome, and Gardner syndrome.

Most sporadic angiosarcomas occur in the breast parenchyma of young females (mean age 35 years) and have a poor prognosis. Tumors occurring after treatment for breast cancer typically arise in older females and are associated with radiation therapy or chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome). After radiation therapy, approximately 0.3% of females develop angiosarcomas in breast skin, with most cases being diagnosed 5 to 10 years after treatment. stromal cellularity, atypia, and mitotic activity.
plification, which can be detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization
and is present in more than 90% of cases.
KEY CONCEPTS
Stromal Tumors
• Intralobular stroma is the origin of two biphasic tumors, fibroadenoma and
phyllodes tumor, which are distinguished based on histological criteria such
as stromal cellularity.
• Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumor of the breast.
• Tumors of interlobular stroma consist only of stromal cells and include both
benign and malignant lesions.
• Angiosarcoma is the most common interlobular stromal malignancy
and can either be sporadic or associated with radiation exposure or
lymphedema.
OTHER MALIGNANT TUMORS OF THE BREAST
Hematolymphoid and cutaneous malignancies, together with breast
metastases from other sites account for less than 5% of malignant
breast tumors. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma may arise primarily in the
breast, or the breasts may be secondarily involved by systemic disease.
Most primary breast lymphomas are of B-cell type, with the most
common subtype being diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (Chapter 13).
While rare, T-cell lymphomas may arise in association with breast
implants (breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma),
possibly due to chronic inflammation, which is known to stimulate
lymphoma development in other contexts. Young females with Burkitt
lymphoma may present with massive bilateral breast involvement,
often while pregnant or lactating. Malignant tumors may arise from
the epidermis and dermis of breast skin; these tumors are identical to
their counterparts found in skin elsewhere (see Chapter 25). Metastases to the breast are rare; the most common culprits are melanoma
and ovarian carcinoma.

Young females with Burkitt lymphoma may present with massive bilateral breast involvement, often while pregnant or lactating. Malignant tumors may arise from the epidermis and dermis of breast skin; these tumors are identical to their counterparts found in skin elsewhere (see Chapter 25). Metastases to the breast are rare; the most common culprits are melanoma and ovarian carcinoma.

KEY CONCEPTS

Stromal Tumors

• Intralobular stroma is the origin of two biphasic tumors, fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor, which are distinguished based on histological criteria such as stromal cellularity.

• Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumor of the breast.

• Tumors of interlobular stroma consist only of stromal cells and include both benign and malignant lesions.

• Angiosarcoma is the most common interlobular stromal malignancy and can either be sporadic or associated with radiation exposure or lymphedema.

OTHER MALIGNANT TUMORS OF THE BREAST

Hematolymphoid and cutaneous malignancies, together with breast metastases from other sites account for less than 5% of malignant breast tumors.
